claims.text: Under simultaneous mechanical and corrosive attack, high-entropy-alloy tribo-corrosion is governed by the dynamic formation and disruption of a dense oxide film.
The governing film may be a spinel-type oxide enriched in elements such as Al and Fe.
An intact oxide film acts as a diffusion barrier that slows ion penetration and corrosion.
An intact oxide film reduces abrasive wear by serving as a lubricious, hard mechanical barrier.
Repeated sliding mechanically removes the oxide film and exposes fresh alloy.
Fresh alloy exposed by film disruption undergoes accelerated corrosion and wear.
The balance between oxide-film regeneration and mechanical removal determines the overall tribo-corrosion degradation rate.
A candidate AlCoCrFeNi- or MgAlTiVFeCo-like alloy initially has a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
The candidate alloy initially has no pre-existing thick or stable oxide layer.
High-temperature annealing in an oxygenated environment can create the intended dense protective oxide film.
The proposed controlled comparison is between pre-oxidized and untreated matched samples under otherwise identical reciprocating sliding in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
Pre-oxidized samples will show lower total degradation than untreated samples.
Pre-oxidized samples will show lower wear depth than untreated samples.
Pre-oxidized samples will show lower corrosion current density than untreated samples.
If mechanical disruption outpaces oxide reformation, both wear and corrosion rates will increase.
The prediction should hold under oxidizing conditions and loads at which the oxide film can partially persist.
The prediction may fail in inert atmospheres, at loads that continuously remove the oxide, or at temperatures where oxide formation is too slow.
Wear depth, friction, corrosion current density, and oxide continuity and composition can be monitored to test the hypothesis.
Failure of an intact pre-formed oxide film to reduce both wear and corrosion relative to the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
